title: The Plural
summary: More than one: the nominative, accusative and genitive plural of nouns, the agreement of adjectives in number, and the cases that numerals govern — which are not the ones an English speaker expects.

rules.heading: The Nominative Plural
rules.statement: The plural has its own endings in every case, and they must be learned beside the singular rather than derived from it. The nominative plural is given below. Note that the masculine ending **-as** makes **-ai**, which is not the *-ai* of the feminine dative, and that **-us** makes **-ūs** with a long vowel.

paradigms.caption: Nominative singular → nominative plural
paradigms.footnote: The feminine plural in -os and -ės is identical to the genitive singular of the same word. Only the sentence tells them apart: *knygos yra naujos* (plural subject) beside *brolio knygos* (genitive singular).

rules.heading: The Accusative Plural
rules.statement: The accusative plural takes **-us** in the masculine and **-as** or **-es** in the feminine. Unlike the singular, it carries **no nosinė hook**: the hook marks the accusative singular and nothing else, so a word ending in a hooked vowel is always singular.

paradigms.caption: Accusative singular → accusative plural
paradigms.footnote: Nouns in -us have the same form in the nominative singular and the accusative plural: *sūnus*. Only the sentence settles which is meant.

rules.heading: The Genitive Plural
rules.statement: The genitive plural ends in **-ų** for every noun of every gender and declension without exception — the one ending in the language that need never be looked up. A soft consonant before it may change: *katė* gives *kačių*, *t* becoming *č*.
footnotes: This is the ending met already in *kilogramas obuolių* (¶32) and *daug pinigų*.

rules.heading: Agreement of the Adjective in Number
rules.statement: An adjective agrees with its noun in **number** as well as in gender and case. The masculine nominative plural is **-i**, the feminine **-os**; in the accusative plural they are **-us** and **-as**, matching the noun's own endings.

paradigms.caption: geras, gera — singular and plural
paradigms.footnote: Adjectives of the other two classes follow suit: *didelis → dideli*, *didelė → didelės*; *gražus → gražūs*, *graži → gražios*.

rules.heading: The Verb and the Plural
rules.statement: The verb was said (¶24) to have **one form for the whole third person**, and the plural does not disturb it: *katė miega* and *katės miega* differ only in the noun. Where the subject is *mes*, *jūs*, *jie* or *jos*, the first- and second-person endings apply as before; the third person alone is indifferent to number.

examples.gloss: The boy works. / The boys work.

rules.heading: The Case a Numeral Governs
rules.statement: A numeral does not simply stand before its noun; it settles that noun's **number and case**. **Vienas** and **two to nine** *decline along with* the noun and agree with it: nominative plural where the phrase is a subject, accusative plural where it is an object. **Ten and upwards**, and every number from eleven to nineteen, do the opposite — they do not agree at all, but freeze the noun in the **genitive plural** whatever case the sentence would otherwise have required. In a compound number the **last word** decides: *dvidešimt vienas namas*, twenty-one houses, has a singular noun after it.

paradigms.caption: Numeral and noun
paradigms.footnote: *vienas* and *du* have feminine forms: *viena knyga*, *dvi knygos*. That a numeral of ten or more keeps its noun in the genitive plural even when the phrase is an object — *matau dešimt namų* — is the point an English speaker finds hardest. The numerals themselves are taken up in full later.

examples.note: accusative plural, the verb governing it
genitive plural after dešimt, whatever the verb wants

drills.stem: What is the nominative plural of **sūnus**?
drills.explanation: Masculine **-us** makes **-ūs** with a long vowel (¶53). *sūnai* wrongly copies the *-as → -ai* pattern; *sūnus* is either nominative singular or accusative plural; *sūnų* is genitive plural.

drills.stem: Complete: **Aš matau naujas ____.** (I see new books.)
drills.explanation: A direct object takes the accusative plural: *knygas*. *naujas* already shows the feminine accusative plural of the adjective (¶56). *knygos* is nominative/genitive singular — the classic subject-for-object slip.

drills.stem: What is the genitive plural of **katė**?
drills.explanation: Every noun takes **-ų** in the genitive plural; here *t* softens to *č* before the ending: *kačių* (¶55). *katės* is nominative plural / genitive singular; *kates* accusative plural; *katėms* dative plural.

drills.stem: Which phrases show **correct** adjective–noun agreement in the plural?
drills.explanation: *knygos* is feminine, so *geri knygos* mismatches gender. The first two are nominative plurals; *gerus namus* is a correct accusative plural (as after *matau*).

drills.stem: Complete: **Ji turi dešimt ____.** (She has ten apples.)
drills.explanation: *dešimt* freezes the noun in the **genitive plural** whatever case *turėti* would otherwise want (¶58). *obuolius* is the accusative plural that *du* or *penki* would leave to the verb — the near-miss.

drills.stem: *Katės miega* and *Katė miega* differ only in the noun. What does that show?
options: That Lithuanian verbs agree with the subject in number.
That the third-person form is indifferent to number.
That *miegoti* is irregular in the plural.
That plural subjects take a different conjugation.
drills.explanation: One third-person form serves singular and plural alike (¶57). First and second persons have separate plural endings; the third does not. *Kates miega* would wrongly put an accusative in subject position.

drills.stem: In which sentences does a numeral **override** the case the verb would otherwise require?
drills.explanation: *dešimt* and *vienuolika* impose genitive plural where *turėti*/*matyti* want accusative. *du* and *penki* force plural number but leave case to the verb — *brolius*, *namus*.

drills.stem: *Knygos* is ambiguous. In **Brolio knygos yra ant stalo**, which reading is forced?
options: nominative plural — the books are the subject
genitive singular — the brother's book(s) as possessed thing
accusative plural — the books are an object
genitive plural — after a quantity word
drills.explanation: *brolio* (genitive) marks possession of what follows, so *knygos* is genitive singular here (¶53 footnote). In *Knygos yra naujos* the same shape would be nominative plural — only the sentence settles it.

drills.stem: Complete: **Aš matau ____ namus.** (I see five houses.)
drills.explanation: Two-to-nine numerals decline and agree: after *matyti* the whole phrase is accusative plural, so **penkis namus** (¶58). *penki* is nominative; *penkių* genitive; *penkios* feminine nominative.

drills.stem: Which forms of **namas** are correctly paired with their case and number?
drills.explanation: *namą* is accusative **singular** (with the nosinė hook). Accusative plural is *namus* and never carries a hook (¶54).

drills.stem: The plurals *namai, broliai, sūnūs, knygos, katės* show how many **different nominative-plural endings**?
drills.explanation: Five endings: *-ai, -iai, -ūs, -os, -ės*.

drills.stem: **Vaikas turi vieną gerą obuolį.** If *vieną* becomes *dešimt*, how many of the five words change form?
drills.explanation: Three: *vieną* → *dešimt*, and *gerą obuolį* → *gerų obuolių* (genitive plural under *dešimt*, adjective agreeing). *Vaikas* and *turi* are untouched — the numeral overrides the object's case, not the subject's.

drills.stem: Nominative plural of **namas**?
drills.explanation: *-as* → **-ai**: *namai* (¶53). *namus* is accusative plural; *namų* genitive plural; *namą* accusative singular with the hook.

drills.stem: Nominative plural of **knyga**?
drills.explanation: Feminine *-a* → **-os**: *knygos* (¶53). *knygas* is accusative plural; *knygų* genitive plural; *knygą* accusative singular.

drills.stem: Accusative plural of **brolis**?
drills.explanation: Masculine *-is* → accusative plural **-ius**: *brolius* (¶54). *broliai* nominative plural; *brolių* genitive; *brolį* accusative singular.

drills.stem: Complete: **Mes turime ____ knygas.** (We have three books.)
drills.explanation: 2–9 decline with the noun: after *turėti* the phrase is accusative plural → **tris knygas** (¶58). *trys* is nominative; genitive forms would follow *reikia* or *dešimt*.

drills.stem: Complete: **Geri ____ skaito.** (Good boys are reading.)
drills.explanation: Subject + agreeing adjective → nominative plural: *geri berniukai* (¶56, ¶53). *berniukus* would be an object; *berniukų* genitive plural.

drills.stem: Complete: **Aš matau didelius ____.** (I see big houses.)
drills.explanation: Object of *matyti* → accusative plural, and the adjective already shows *-us*: **didelius namus** (¶54, ¶56). *namai* is nominative — the classic subject-for-object slip.

drills.stem: Which are **correct** genitive plurals?
drills.explanation: Every noun takes **-ų**; *katė* softens *t*→*č* → *kačių*, not *katų* (¶55).

drills.stem: Which sentences keep **third-person** verb form the same in singular and plural?
drills.explanation: Third person is number-indifferent (¶57). First person changes: *dirbu* / *dirbame*.

drills.stem: Complete: **Mokytojas mato ____ vaikų.** (The teacher sees ten children.)
drills.explanation: *dešimt* and upwards freeze the noun in genitive plural and the numeral itself does not agree: **dešimt vaikų** (¶58). Declined *dešimtį* would be wrong here.

drills.stem: *sūnus* can be nominative singular **or** accusative plural. Which sentence forces the **plural** reading?
drills.explanation: After *matau* an object is needed → accusative plural *sūnus* (¶54 footnote). The others treat *sūnus* as a singular subject.

drills.stem: Which phrases are **correct** after *turėti*?
drills.explanation: 2–9 leave case to the verb (*du brolius*, *penkis obuolius*); *dešimt* overrides to genitive plural (*knygų*), so *dešimt knygas* is the near-miss (¶58).

drills.stem: Feminine accusative plural of **naujas** + **knyga**?
drills.explanation: Adjective and noun both take feminine accusative plural: **naujas knygas** (¶56). *naujos knygos* is nominative; *naujų knygų* follows quantity words.

drills.stem: Which of these are **nominative plural**?
drills.explanation: *namai*, *knygos*, and *sūnūs* are nominative plural. *namus* is accusative plural.

drills.stem: **Aš turiu penkis gerus obuolius.** If *penkis* is replaced by *dešimt*, how many words must change form?
drills.explanation: Four: *penkis* → *dešimt*, *gerus* → *gerų*, *obuolius* → *obuolių*. *Aš* and *turiu* stay. Under *dešimt* the counted phrase goes genitive plural.

drills.stem: The genitive plurals *namų, knygų, kačių* all end in the same letter. How many **letters** is that shared ending?
drills.explanation: One letter: **-ų**. Softening (*katė* → *kačių*) changes the stem, not the ending.

drills.title: Mokykloje
drills.passage: Tai mokykla. Čia dirba geri mokytojai. Vaikai skaito naujas knygas. Ant stalų guli daiktai: knygos, laiškai, obuoliai. Vienas berniukas turi du obuolius, o mergaitė turi dešimt knygų. Mokytojos yra jaunos ir geros. Vaikai jų klauso. Penki berniukai žaidžia, o trys mergaitės skaito. Mokytojas mato septynis vaikus.
drills.translation: This is a school. Good teachers work here. The children are reading new books. On the tables lie things: books, letters, apples. One boy has two apples, and a girl has ten books. The (female) teachers are young and good. The children listen to them. Five boys are playing, and three girls are reading. The teacher sees seven children.

questions.explanation: *Vaikai skaito naujas knygas* — accusative plural object. *naujos knygos* is nominative and could only be a subject; *naujų knygų* would follow *dešimt* or *daug*.

questions.stem: Which of these does the passage support **and** state grammatically?
questions.explanation: The third is ungrammatical: *dešimt* requires *knygų*. The passage actually has the correct genitive plural.

questions.stem: How many **children** does the teacher see (as a bare number)?
questions.explanation: *Mokytojas mato septynis vaikus* — seven. Note *septynis vaikus*: 2–9 agree in the accusative plural; had it been *dešimt*, the noun would have been *vaikų*.

questions.stem: In **Penki berniukai žaidžia**, why is *berniukai* nominative plural rather than genitive plural?
options: Because 2–9 agree with a plural noun in the case the sentence requires — here nominative as subject.
Because masculine nouns never take genitive plural after numerals.
questions.explanation: *penki* (2–9) declines along with the noun; as subject that is nominative plural. Genitive plural would be forced by *dešimt* and upwards (¶58).

questions.stem: The passage has **du obuolius**. If *du* became *dešimt*, how many words would change form?
questions.explanation: Two: *du* → *dešimt*, *obuolius* → *obuolių*. The subject and verb stay put.
